note.explanation: Data science uses data to understand problems and make better decisions. It brings together computer science, mathematics and statistics, and business knowledge. A data science workflow moves from identifying a problem to collecting, cleaning, analysing, interpreting, and visualizing data.
examples: A school collects students’ arrival times, checks the data for errors, looks for patterns, works out likely reasons for lateness, and presents the results in a chart.
A sports team analyses performance data to find patterns and develop better strategies.
note.simple: Data science is detective work with data: find information, check it, look for clues, understand what they mean, and show the results clearly.
note.checkQuestion: In the workflow, what step comes after data collection?
note.title: How data science turns data into insights
steps: Identify and clearly define the problem.
Clean the data by fixing errors and organizing it.
Analyse the data to look for patterns or answers.
Interpret the results and draw conclusions.
Visualize the data with charts or graphs to make it easier to understand.
note.answer: Data science combines computer skills, math, and business knowledge to turn raw data into useful insights.

options: To turn raw data into useful insights
To make data harder to understand
To replace all decisions with guesses
To collect information without a problem to solve

rationales: Incorrect: analysis happens after the problem is defined and data is collected and cleaned.
Correct: the workflow begins by understanding and clearly defining the problem.
Incorrect: visualization is used later to communicate results.
Incorrect: cleaning follows data collection, not problem identification.

options: Removing errors and organizing the collected data
Making a chart before gathering any information

Incorrect: a chart is a form of visualization, and this option places it before collecting data.
Incorrect: deciding what results mean is data interpretation.
Incorrect: choosing and defining the problem is problem identification.

options: Explaining what the analysed results mean
rationales: Incorrect: looking for patterns or answers is data analysis.
Correct: interpretation means understanding analysed results and drawing conclusions.

options: It makes data easier to understand using charts and graphs

It guarantees that every conclusion is correct

rationales: Correct: charts and graphs can present data in a way that is easier to understand.

rationales: Correct: computer science helps with handling and organizing data.
Incorrect: business knowledge helps apply insights to real-life problems and decisions.

mcqs.stem: A student makes a bar chart to show which sports are most popular. Which workflow step is this?
rationales: Incorrect: collection is gathering the information, such as by conducting a survey.
Incorrect: interpretation is understanding the results and drawing conclusions.
Incorrect: cleaning is fixing errors and organizing the collected information.
Correct: making a chart to communicate data is data visualization.

written.text: Describe the process of conducting a survey to gather data about students' favourite extracurricular activities.
written.finalAnswer: Define the question, collect survey responses, clean and organize the data, analyse it, interpret the results, and present them using a suitable chart.

rubric.why: The workflow begins with a clearly defined problem or question.
rubric.description: Identify what the survey needs to find out.
rubric.how: State that the aim is to find students’ favourite extracurricular activities.

rubric.why: Responses must be gathered before they can be analysed.
rubric.how: Explain that students answer a survey and their responses are gathered.

rubric.why: Errors should be fixed and the data organized before analysis.
rubric.how: Say that responses are checked, errors corrected, and data organized.

rubric.why: A complete process includes making sense of the results and communicating them.
rubric.description: Analyse, interpret, and present the survey findings.
rubric.how: Explain that responses are analysed, conclusions are drawn, and findings are shown clearly.

modelAnswer: Clearly define the question: which extracurricular activities do students like best?
Collect data by asking students to complete a survey about their favourite activities.
Clean the data by checking responses, fixing errors, and organizing the information.
Analyse the responses to find patterns, such as which activities receive the most choices.
Interpret the results and draw a conclusion about students’ preferences.
Use a suitable chart, such as a bar chart, to show the results clearly.

written.finalAnswer: Data visualization presents data in charts or graphs to make it easier to understand. For example, a bar chart can compare students’ sports preferences, and a line graph can show how a value changes over time.

written.text: Differentiate between nominal, ordinal, discrete, and continuous data. For each type, describe a suitable visualization technique and provide a specific example of how this technique can be used to represent that type of data effectively.
written.finalAnswer: Nominal data names categories without order and can be shown with a bar or pie chart; ordinal data has ordered categories and can be shown with a bar chart; discrete data consists of countable separate values and can be shown with a histogram or dot plot; continuous data can take measured values across a range and can be shown with a line graph, scatter plot, or box plot.

rubric.why: Nominal data is categorized without order, and the answer needs an appropriate visual example.
rubric.description: Explain nominal data and give a suitable visualization.
rubric.how: Describe unordered categories and name a bar chart or pie chart with a fitting example.

rubric.why: Ordinal categories have an order, which should be reflected in the answer.
rubric.description: Explain ordinal data and give a suitable visualization.
rubric.how: Describe ordered categories and name a bar chart or stacked bar chart with a fitting example.

rubric.why: Discrete data consists of countable separate values and needs a suitable representation.
rubric.description: Explain discrete data and give a suitable visualization.
rubric.how: Describe countable values and name a dot plot or histogram with a fitting example.

rubric.why: The final point must correctly describe continuous data and give an appropriate visualization.
rubric.description: Explain continuous data and give a suitable visualization.
rubric.how: Describe measured values across a range and name a line graph, scatter plot, or box plot with a fitting example.

modelAnswer: Nominal data places items into categories without implying an order; a bar chart or pie chart can show students’ favourite sports.
Ordinal data has categories with an order; a bar chart can show ratings such as low, medium, and high.
Discrete data has distinct, countable values; a dot plot or histogram can show the number of students absent each day.
Continuous data is measured and can take values across a range; a line graph can show students’ heights or another measurement.

examTips: A short question may ask you to define data science or explain why data visualization is useful. Give a direct meaning and one clear benefit.

A question may ask you to put the data science workflow in order. Keep the book’s sequence: problem identification, data collection, data cleaning, data analysis, data interpretation, and data visualization.
In a longer answer, explain what happens at each relevant step and use a simple example, such as investigating why students arrive late.
Marks are earned by naming the correct fields or workflow steps, explaining their purpose, and using a relevant example.
Do not mix up analysis (looking for patterns) and interpretation (understanding the results and drawing conclusions).

steps.why: This is the problem the school wants to investigate.
steps.text: Imagine a school wants to understand why some students arrive late.

steps.why: Arrival times are gathered as the information needed for the investigation.
steps.text: They start by collecting data on arrival times (data collection).

steps.why: Errors must be corrected before the data is useful.
steps.text: Next, they clean the data by fixing any errors (data cleaning).

steps.why: The school looks through the data for possible causes and patterns.
steps.text: They then analyse the data to find patterns, like whether bad weather or traffic is causing the delays (data analysis).

steps.why: The school works out what the patterns mean.
steps.text: They interpret these patterns to understand why students are late (data interpretation).

steps.why: A chart communicates the findings in a clear visual form.
steps.text: Finally, they create a chart to show the most common reasons for being late (data visualization).

steps.why: This sums up how the steps work together as a process.
steps.text: This entire process of collecting, cleaning, analysing, interpreting, and visualizing data is what data science is all about!

example.question: Imagine a school wants to understand why some students arrive late.
example.answer: The school collects and cleans arrival-time data, analyses it for patterns, interprets the patterns, and creates a chart to show the most common reasons for lateness.

explain.title: What data science does
explain.body: Data science is like being a detective, but instead of solving crimes, you solve problems using data. It combines computer skills, math, and business knowledge to turn raw data into useful insights.

explain.title: Why data science is useful
explain.body: Data science helps people make better decisions. Businesses can learn what customers like, sports teams can improve strategies, and doctors can predict health trends and provide better care.

explain.title: Different fields work together
explain.body: Computer Science: For handling and organizing data. Mathematics and Statistics: For analysing data and finding patterns. Business Knowledge: For applying these insights to real-life problems and making informed decisions.

explain.title: The data science workflow
explain.body: Data Science Workflow, refers to the systematic process used by data scientists to extract insights and knowledge from data. The steps are problem identification, data collection, data cleaning, data analysis, data interpretation, and data visualization.

explain.title: The last steps make findings useful
explain.body: Analysis looks closely at data to find patterns or answers. Interpretation means understanding the analysed data and drawing conclusions. Visualization uses charts and graphs to make data easier to understand.

mistakes: Starting the workflow with data collection instead of problem identification.
Confusing data analysis (finding patterns) with data interpretation (understanding results and drawing conclusions).
Treating data cleaning as the same as collecting data; cleaning means fixing errors and organizing data after collection.
Saying that visualization is only decoration; charts and graphs help people understand data.
Listing the fields of data science without explaining their roles: computer science handles and organizes data, mathematics and statistics analyse it, and business knowledge applies insights.
